To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the extent of metal (Co and Cr) release from CoCrMO alloy is dependent on applied potential and the presence of oxygen in the solution, and that the presence of BSA may accelerate metal release, however this effect was not possible to quantify due to precipitation of metal-proteins.
Co is preferentially released from CoCrMo at no applied potential, while Cr is released as Cr(III) in PBS and Cr(VI) at applied potentials in PBS + H 2 O 2, but not in PBS.
Cr(III) and Cr(VI) were the main released species from CoCrMo alloy in PBS, while Co, Cr(II), Cr(III), and Cr(VI), as well as Mo, were released from AISI 316 L.
In summary, our research is concerned with
metal release from Co-Cr-Mo alloys, which is a key issue for their use in biomedical applications.
the release and speciation (i.e., Cr(III), Mo, Co, Cr(VI), CoCrMo, and 316L) from biomedical alloys into simulated physiological solutions (i.e., PBS, PBS + H2O2, and PBS + BSA).
the release and speciation from a CoCrMo alloy in physiologically relevant media.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the release of metals from the CoCrM alloy was dependent on the applied potential and the presence of oxygen in the solution.
the extent of released Cr(VI) is negligible at no applied potential, and that the extent of Cr(VI) and Cr(III) release is dependent on the applied potential and the solution chemistry.
BSA does not enhance metal release but rather that the presence of BSA in solution may result in the precipitation of metal complexes, thereby underestimating the actual metal release.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Cr release from CoCrM alloy was limited by the presence of an outer Cr-enriched surface oxide.
Cr(VI) was released from CoCrMo in PBS and PBS + H2O2 at applied potential.
Cr(VI) is not released from CoCrMo under physiologically relevant conditions and that Co is the metal preferentially released at no applied potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Cr(III) is the primary species released from CoCrMo in PBS, while Cr(VI) is the primary released species from CoCrMo at applied potentials.
Cr(VI) is only formed from a CoCrMo alloy under anodic polarization, and that the extent of metal and Cr(VI) released from the Co-CrMo alloy is significantly lower than that from 316L.
metal release from Co-based alloys may be affected by applied potentials, the presence of H2 O2 and BSA, and the formation of metal-protein complex precipitates.
